stem: A developer moved the team's instructions from ./CLAUDE.md to ./.claude/CLAUDE.md. In a new Claude Code session, Claude no longer seems to follow the conventions, and she wants to confirm whether the file is actually loaded before rewriting anything. What should she do?

options.text: Run /context and check whether the file appears under Memory files.
options.why: /context shows what is in the current context window, including which CLAUDE.md and rules files loaded, so it confirms or rules out a loading problem.

options.text: Run /init so Claude regenerates the project CLAUDE.md from the codebase.
options.why: /init proposes content for a CLAUDE.md; it does not show whether the existing file loaded, and it may change instructions she has not yet diagnosed.

options.text: Run /compact so Claude re-reads the instruction files and applies them again.
options.why: /compact summarizes the conversation to free space; it is not a way to check which instruction files are in context.

options.text: Add an @.claude/CLAUDE.md import to her ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file to force the file to load.
options.why: This changes her personal configuration before confirming the cause, and it would not help teammates if the real problem is the file's content.

explanation: Built-in slash commands support troubleshooting. A project CLAUDE.md can live at ./CLAUDE.md or ./.claude/CLAUDE.md, and /context lists the memory files loaded into the current session. Confirm what loaded before editing: if the file is listed, the problem is how the instructions are written, not where the file is.
reference: Claude Code docs — Memory (troubleshoot CLAUDE.md); Commands

stem: A CI job runs claude -p to triage failing tests. The same commit gives different results on different runners. One runner has a leftover ~/.claude directory with a personal hook and CLAUDE.md, and the MCP server listed in the project's .mcp.json is reachable only from some runners. The team wants every run to use only the configuration the job passes explicitly. What should they do?

options.text: Add a line to the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to ignore personal hooks and unavailable MCP servers.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is guidance for the model; hooks and MCP connections are loaded by Claude Code itself and are not switched off by instructions.

options.text: Run with --bare and supply what the job needs through flags such as --settings and --mcp-config.
options.why: Bare mode skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so each run loads only what the command line supplies.

options.text: Add --output-format json so every runner returns results in the same structure.
options.why: The output format changes how results are returned, not which hooks, instructions and servers are loaded for the run.

options.text: Add --dangerously-skip-permissions so that hooks and permission prompts can no longer affect the run.
options.why: Skipping permission checks does not stop hooks, CLAUDE.md or MCP servers from loading, and it removes safeguards from the CI job.

explanation: Without --bare, claude -p loads the same context an interactive session would, including anything in ~/.claude and the working directory. For CI and scripts that must behave the same on every machine, --bare skips that auto-discovery; the job supplies settings, MCP servers, agents and prompt additions through flags. Bare mode authenticates with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or an apiKeyHelper) rather than a subscription login.
reference: Claude Code docs — Run Claude Code programmatically (bare mode)

stem: A CI job must run Claude Code non-interactively to list the functions changed in a pull request and pass the result to a script that expects a JSON object with a "functions" array. What is the most reliable way to invoke it?

options.text: Start an interactive session in the CI runner and export the transcript once Claude has finished the task.
options.why: Interactive mode waits for terminal input and is not designed for unattended CI runs or machine-readable output.

options.text: Run claude -p with the default text output and parse the reply with a regular expression.
options.why: Free-form text has no guaranteed structure, so regex parsing is brittle.

options.text: Run claude -p with --output-format json and a --json-schema that defines the functions array.
options.why: Print mode with JSON output and a schema returns validated structured output in the response payload, which scripts can parse reliably.

options.text: Run claude --continue in the CI runner so it picks up the previous pull request's session.
options.why: --continue resumes an earlier conversation; it neither makes the run non-interactive nor defines an output format.

explanation: Headless (print) mode, claude -p, runs a prompt without the interactive UI. --output-format controls the result shape (text, json, or stream-json), and pairing json with --json-schema returns structured output that conforms to the schema for downstream scripts.
reference: Claude Code docs — Run Claude Code programmatically (headless)

stem: A developer is scripting around Claude Code and needs to manage sessions and stream output. Which two statements about Claude Code CLI behavior are accurate? (Choose two.)

options.text: --output-format stream-json returns one JSON object after the run completes.
options.why: stream-json emits newline-delimited JSON events as the run progresses; the single-object form is --output-format json.

options.text: claude --continue loads the most recent conversation in the current directory.
options.why: --continue (-c) picks up the latest conversation for the directory, which is convenient for iterating on the same task.

options.text: Using --fork-session with --resume permanently deletes the original session's history.
options.why: --fork-session creates a new session ID when resuming and leaves the original session intact.

options.text: claude --resume accepts a session ID or name to reopen a specific earlier session.
options.why: --resume (-r) targets a specific session by ID or name, or shows a picker when no value is given.

options.text: claude -p opens a REPL that keeps waiting for follow-up prompts after it answers.
options.why: Print mode answers and exits; follow-ups are sent as new runs, for example with --continue or --resume.

explanation: Claude Code sessions persist, so --continue reopens the latest conversation in the directory and --resume reopens a chosen one (optionally forked with --fork-session). For programmatic consumers, -p runs once and exits, json returns a final object, and stream-json streams newline-delimited events.

stem: A team has a 25-step release procedure with helper scripts. They want to trigger it by typing /release, and they also want Claude to pick it up automatically when someone asks to "cut a release." They do not want the procedure loaded into context during unrelated work. Which Claude Code component fits best?

options.text: Paste the procedure into the project CLAUDE.md so Claude always knows the steps.
options.why: CLAUDE.md content loads into every session, spending context on unrelated work, and it does not create a /release command.

options.text: A project skill in .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md with a clear description and its helper scripts.
options.why: A skill is invocable as /release, can bundle supporting files, and loads automatically only when its description matches the request.

options.text: A path-scoped rule in .claude/rules/ whose paths frontmatter matches the release scripts directory.
options.why: Path-scoped rules load when Claude reads matching files; they do not create a command or respond to a request to cut a release.

options.text: A custom subagent defined in .claude/agents/ whose system prompt contains the full release procedure.
options.why: Subagents are for delegating work to a separate context; they do not provide the /release command the team wants.

explanation: Skills package reusable procedures with optional supporting files. The skill name becomes a slash command, and the description lets Claude load it on demand. Custom commands in .claude/commands/ still work, but skills add supporting files and automatic invocation. CLAUDE.md and rules are for standing guidance, and subagents are for delegated work.

stem: A developer is running a long refactor in Claude Code on her own laptop, not in a container. Constant permission prompts are slowing her down, but she still wants protection against clearly risky actions. Which permission mode best fits?

options.text: bypassPermissions, so that no tool call ever prompts for approval during the refactor.
options.why: bypassPermissions skips checks entirely and is intended for isolated containers or VMs, not a personal machine.

options.text: plan, so Claude can explore the codebase without asking.
options.why: Plan mode is for analysis before editing; it does not let Claude carry out the refactor.

options.text: auto, where a classifier model reviews actions in place of most permission prompts.
options.why: Auto mode is designed for long tasks and prompt fatigue: a separate classifier blocks risky actions while routine ones proceed without prompts.

options.text: dontAsk, so that anything not pre-approved is skipped silently instead of prompting.
options.why: dontAsk denies every action that would otherwise prompt, so the refactor would stall on unapproved commands.

explanation: Claude Code permission modes trade convenience for oversight: default (Manual) asks for most actions, acceptEdits auto-approves file edits, plan is read-only analysis, auto runs with background safety checks, dontAsk allows only pre-approved actions, and bypassPermissions skips checks for isolated environments. Deny rules still apply on top of any mode.

stem: A monorepo's CLAUDE.md has grown to about 800 lines. It covers frontend conventions, backend API rules, and several long runbooks. Developers report that Claude follows instructions less reliably and that frontend rules clutter backend sessions. Which two changes best address this? (Choose two.)

options.text: Split the file into several documents and pull them back in with @path imports.
options.why: Imported files are expanded and loaded at launch, so the same content still fills the context.

options.text: Move area-specific guidance into .claude/rules/ files that use paths frontmatter.
options.why: Path-scoped rules load when Claude works with matching files, keeping frontend guidance out of backend sessions.

options.text: Move the whole file to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md so it no longer counts against the project.
options.why: User-level instructions still load into every session, and the team would lose the shared, versioned file.

options.text: Turn the long runbooks into skills that load on demand, and keep CLAUDE.md short.
options.why: Skills load their full content only when invoked or relevant, so runbooks stop consuming context in every session.

options.text: Convert the instructions into keys in .claude/settings.json so they are enforced.
options.why: settings.json configures permissions, hooks, models and similar options; it is not a place for natural-language coding conventions.

explanation: Large CLAUDE.md files consume context and reduce adherence. Keep always-on instructions concise, scope area-specific guidance with path-based rules, and move procedures into on-demand skills. Imports help organization but do not reduce what loads at launch.
reference: Claude Code docs — Memory (CLAUDE.md, rules, imports)
